passages.title: Measuring the energy in food
paragraphs: A bomb calorimeter burns a weighed sample in excess oxygen inside a sealed steel vessel of fixed volume, immersed in a stirred water bath. Because the volume cannot change, the sample does no work against its surroundings and every joule released appears as heat, so what the instrument measures is the internal energy change rather than the enthalpy change. For solids and liquids the two differ by too little to matter in nutritional work. The heat is found from q = C ΔT, where C is the heat capacity of the whole assembly and ΔT the rise in bath temperature.

The assembly is calibrated before use by burning 1.000 g of benzoic acid, whose heat of combustion is known accurately as 26.4 kJ/g. In one laboratory the standard raised the bath by 2.64 °C. Four 1.00 g samples were then burned in the calibrated instrument: glucose, casein, ethanol and palmitic acid, a saturated 16-carbon fatty acid. Table 1 records the temperature rise each produced.

How much energy a food releases per gram depends on how reduced its carbon atoms are. Combustion converts C-H and C-C bonds into C=O and O-H bonds, and a carbon already bonded to oxygen has less of that conversion left to give. A fatty acid is a long hydrocarbon chain with a single carboxyl group; a carbohydrate carries an oxygen on almost every carbon.

Figures measured this way exceed the energy a body can extract. Digestion is incomplete, and the nitrogen of a protein leaves the body as urea rather than being oxidised, so a calorimeter credits protein with energy the body never collects.

passages.title: Breathing thin air
paragraphs: Dry air is 21% oxygen wherever one stands; what changes with altitude is the total pressure. Gas reaching the alveoli has been warmed to body temperature and fully saturated with water vapour, which contributes 47 mmHg of the total whatever the barometric pressure happens to be. By Dalton's law each gas in a mixture exerts a pressure proportional to its share of the molecules, so the partial pressure of oxygen in humidified inspired gas is the oxygen fraction multiplied by the barometric pressure after the water vapour has been taken out.

Oxygen is diluted again inside the alveolus by carbon dioxide arriving from the blood. The alveolar gas equation accounts for that dilution: alveolar PO₂ equals the humidified inspired value minus PaCO₂ divided by R, where PaCO₂ is the arterial carbon dioxide pressure and R the respiratory exchange ratio, close to 0.8 on a mixed diet.

A research team compared arterial blood gases in volunteers at sea level with those in volunteers at a clinic 4000 m higher (Table 1). The altitude group had been resident for a week, long enough for ventilation to rise and arterial carbon dioxide to settle at a new, lower value.

The same team studied the air transport of patients with a closed pneumothorax. Gas trapped in the pleural space sits at the pressure of its surroundings and contains a fixed quantity of gas, so as the ambient pressure falls the pocket expands, at constant temperature, according to Boyle's law. A pocket measured at 20 mL at sea level is carried up to the same clinic.

figure.caption: Table 1  Barometric pressure and measured arterial carbon dioxide at the two sites.

passages.title: Titrating an amino acid
paragraphs: Histidine carries three ionisable groups: the alpha-carboxyl group with a pKa of 1.8, the imidazole side chain at 6.0, and the alpha-amino group at 9.2. A 25.0 mL sample of 0.100 M histidine hydrochloride, fully protonated at the start, was titrated with 0.100 M sodium hydroxide while the pH was recorded continuously. Figure 1 shows the curve.

Each group accepts one equivalent of base, and the titrant and the analyte are at the same concentration, so equivalence points fall at 25.0, 50.0 and 75.0 mL. Between them the pH climbs slowly. At the midpoint of each rise the protonated and deprotonated forms of the group being titrated are present in equal amounts, so the relation pH = pKa + log([A-]/[HA]) collapses to pH = pKa. Buffering is strongest at those midpoints and weakest at an equivalence point, where essentially one form remains and a small further addition of base moves the pH sharply.

The isoelectric point is the pH at which the molecule carries no net charge. For an amino acid whose side chain is basic it lies halfway between the pKa values of the two groups that bracket the neutral species, not halfway along the titration. A neutral histidine molecule has lost the carboxyl proton and still holds the amino proton, while its side chain may be protonated or not; averaging the two pKa values that bracket that species is what locates the pH at which the positive and negative charges balance across the population.

Which group is responsible for which rise cannot be read off the curve alone. A student proposed repeating the titration with an analogue in which the imidazole ring has been replaced by an unreactive methyl group, keeping everything else the same.

passages.title: Assaying vitamin C in a tablet
paragraphs: Ascorbic acid is a two-electron reducing agent. Oxidation converts it to dehydroascorbic acid, releasing two protons and two electrons, and an iodine molecule takes both of those electrons as it is reduced to two iodide ions. One mole of ascorbic acid therefore consumes exactly one mole of iodine. The endpoint is signalled by starch, which forms an intense blue complex with the first trace of iodine left unreacted.

A tablet was crushed, dissolved and made up to 100.0 mL with water that had been boiled and cooled. Boiling matters: dissolved oxygen oxidises ascorbic acid slowly in solution, and any that is lost that way never reaches the burette. A 25.00 mL aliquot was acidified and titrated with 0.0100 M iodine solution, and the titration was repeated three times (Table 1).

The iodine solution was standardised against a weighed sample of sodium thiosulfate on the morning of the assay, because an iodine solution does not keep: iodine escapes slowly from the solution, and traces of air convert iodide back to iodine in the reverse direction. Starch was added only as the endpoint approached, since starch is itself slowly oxidised by iodine and, in the presence of a large excess of iodine, the blue complex releases its iodine sluggishly and blurs the endpoint.

The formula mass of ascorbic acid, C₆H₈O₆, is 176.1 g/mol. Assays of this kind measure total reducing capacity rather than ascorbic acid specifically, so a tablet containing another reducing agent will read high. A label that overstates the vitamin content of a supplement is a common finding in surveys of the market, and an assay that measures reducing capacity rather than ascorbic acid specifically cannot distinguish an honest tablet from one fortified with a cheaper reductant.

passages.title: Spinning a sample down
paragraphs: A centrifuge creates no new force. It places a sample in a rotating frame, where the only way a particle can follow a circle is for the fluid around it to push it inward. A particle denser than the medium cannot be pushed inward hard enough to keep up, and so drifts outward, toward the bottom of the tube. The inward acceleration required is a = ω² r, with ω the angular velocity in radians per second and r the distance from the axis of rotation. Laboratories report this as a relative centrifugal force: the ratio of ω² r to g.

Angular velocity follows from the rotor speed, ω = 2 π f, where f is the number of revolutions each second, so a speed quoted in revolutions per minute has to be divided by 60 before it is used. Because the radius enters once and the speed twice, doubling the speed changes the field four times as much as doubling the radius does.
A laboratory compares four protocols on the same benchtop machine (Table 1), first separating plasma from cells and then platelets from plasma. Take g as 9.8 m/s².

How fast a given particle actually settles depends on more than the field. A larger or denser particle in a less viscous medium settles faster, and two populations of nearly equal density separate poorly however hard the rotor is driven, because the difference in their sedimentation rates, not the rate itself, is what sets them apart. Protocols for such pairs run long and moderate, often with the sample layered over a density gradient so that each population halts where the gradient matches its own density. A swinging-bucket rotor is preferred when the boundary between two layers has to stay flat enough to pipette.

passages.title: Measuring blood velocity with ultrasound
paragraphs: Doppler ultrasound sends a pulse of frequency f₀ into tissue and listens for the echo returned by moving red cells. The sound is shifted once as it meets a moving target and again as the echo returns to a stationary probe, so the shift appears twice over: Δf = 2 f₀ v cosθ / c, where v is the speed of the blood, θ the angle between the beam and the direction of flow, and c the speed of sound in soft tissue, 1540 m/s. The instrument reports the velocity it computes, not the shift it measures.

The angle is the weak point of the method. At θ = 90° the cosine is zero and flow is invisible however fast it runs, which is why an operator tilts the probe to look along a vessel rather than across it. Clinical practice keeps θ at or below 60°, where the cosine is 0.50 and a small error in the recorded angle costs comparatively little.
A technician using a 5.0 MHz probe records the peak shift from four vessels, holding the beam at θ = 60° throughout (Table 1).

Choosing the probe involves a second compromise. The finest detail the beam can resolve along its own direction is set by the wavelength, so a higher frequency gives a sharper image; but attenuation in tissue rises with frequency, so a higher-frequency probe cannot see as deep. Abdominal work uses 2–3 MHz probes, while superficial vessels in the neck or wrist are imaged at 7–12 MHz.

figure.caption: Table 1  Peak Doppler shift recorded from each vessel at a beam angle of 60°.

passages.title: Choosing a radionuclide
paragraphs: Radioactive decay is a first-order process: the number of nuclei decaying each second is proportional to the number present, so the activity left after a time t is the initial activity multiplied by one half raised to the power t/T, where T is the half-life, and the decay constant is k = ln 2 / T. The constant belongs to the nucleus alone. Warming the sample, binding the atom into a different molecule or injecting it into a patient changes nothing about it, which is what makes a tracer's timetable predictable.

An imaging nuclide has to satisfy several demands at once. Its photons must be energetic enough to leave the body and reach a detector. It must decay fast enough that the dose to the patient does not continue for days after the picture has been taken, and slowly enough to survive preparation, delivery and the scan itself. Positron emitters serve positron emission tomography, where the two 511 keV photons released when a positron annihilates are detected in coincidence. Pure gamma emitters serve single-photon imaging. Beta particles are absorbed within a few millimetres of tissue: they deposit dose without contributing to the image, which makes them valuable in therapy and a liability in diagnosis.

Table 1 lists four nuclides in routine use. Technetium-99m is eluted from a generator in the hospital's own radiopharmacy; fluorine-18 is made in a cyclotron and shipped, and a vial is assayed on arrival; gallium-68 comes from a bedside generator because its half-life leaves no time for transport at all.
A vial of a fluorine-18 tracer is assayed at 400 MBq. The scanner is occupied, and the patient is not injected until 220 minutes later.

figure.caption: Table 1  Half-life and emissions of four nuclides used in imaging and therapy.

passages.title: Keeping alveoli open
paragraphs: A molecule at the surface of a liquid has fewer neighbours to attract it than one in the bulk, so a surface behaves as though it were under tension and shrinks to the smallest area available. For a spherical film of liquid enclosing gas, the pressure inside exceeds the pressure outside by P = 2γ/r, Laplace's law, where γ is the surface tension and r the radius. The thin film of fluid lining an alveolus therefore pulls it inward, and the smaller the alveolus the harder that pull.

Pulmonary surfactant, a mixture of phospholipids and protein secreted by type II alveolar cells, lowers the tension of that film. Its molecules are amphipathic: the hydrophobic tails project into the gas, the head groups stay in the water, and the hydrogen-bonded network at the surface is interrupted wherever one of them sits. Table 1 gives measured values for a saline-lined model alveolus and for a surfactant-lined one at two radii. Treat the pressures as gauge pressures, measured relative to the space outside the alveolus.

The striking property of surfactant is that its tension is not fixed. As an alveolus shrinks the film is compressed, the molecules crowd together and the tension falls further; on inflation the film is stretched, the surfactant is spread thin and the tension rises again. Table 1 shows both states.

That variability is what keeps a lung of unequal alveoli stable. Consider two alveoli of different radii sharing a duct. At a fixed tension, Laplace's law puts the smaller one at the higher pressure, so it would empty into the larger and collapse. A tension that falls as the radius falls works against that, holding the pressures closer together. Infants born before surfactant production begins suffer exactly the predicted failure, and are treated with surfactant instilled into the airway.

passages.title: Delivering a shock
paragraphs: A defibrillator stores energy in a capacitor and releases it through the chest in a few milliseconds. A capacitor held at a potential difference V carries a charge Q = CV and stores an energy U = (1/2) C V². Because the energy goes as the square of the voltage, the charging voltage sets the dose far more sharply than the capacitance does, and a machine changes its setting by charging to a different voltage rather than by switching capacitors.

The discharge path is the patient. Resistance between the pads is typically close to 50 ohm, so the current falls away with a time constant equal to the product of that resistance and the capacitance. Clinicians speak of the dose in joules, but it is current through the myocardium that interrupts a fibrillating rhythm, so a patient whose thoracic impedance is high receives less current from the same stored energy. Modern units measure impedance between the pads before discharging and reshape the waveform to compensate.

Table 1 lists the capacitor modules of one machine, all discharging through the same 50 ohm. The adult module is charged to 2.0 kV for its standard setting, and reaches its 100 J and 360 J settings by charging to 1.4 kV and 2.7 kV instead. A service engineer may wire the two adult capacitors together in parallel.

Capacitors in parallel share the same voltage, and their capacitances add, because the arrangement amounts to one capacitor with the plate area of both. In series the reciprocals add, so a pair behaves as half of one, and the applied voltage divides between them. Either arrangement changes the time constant of the discharge as well as the energy stored, which is why a modified machine has to be re-characterised before use.

figure.caption: Table 1  Capacitor modules of one defibrillator, each discharging through 50 ohm.

passages.title: How a drug meets glutathione
paragraphs: Electrophilic drugs and drug metabolites are detoxified in the liver by conjugation with glutathione, a tripeptide whose cysteine thiol supplies the nucleophile. A candidate drug carrying a primary alkyl bromide was mixed with a model thiol in buffer at pH 7.4 and 37 °C, and the initial rate of conjugate formation was measured at four combinations of concentration (Table 1).

A rate law of the form rate = k[RBr]^m[RSH]^n is established by changing one concentration at a time and watching what the rate does. The exponents are properties of the mechanism rather than of the balanced equation, and in a substitution at saturated carbon they separate the two limiting pathways. In a bimolecular displacement the nucleophile attacks the carbon bearing the leaving group from the side opposite that group, and the new bond forms as the carbon-bromine bond breaks, so both species appear in the rate-determining step. In a unimolecular pathway the leaving group departs first, in a slow step involving the substrate alone, and the carbocation that results is captured afterwards by whatever nucleophile is at hand.
A tertiary analogue of the same drug was then studied under identical conditions. It reacted about thirty times faster, and its rate did not change when the thiol concentration was doubled.

The distinction matters in toxicology. A drug that reacts by the bimolecular route is cleared at a rate proportional to the glutathione available, so clearance slows as the store is depleted but the drug itself is not activated into anything worse. A drug that ionises first is consumed at a rate depletion cannot slow, and the carbocation it forms will react with whatever nucleophile it meets, including the nitrogen atoms of DNA bases.

questions.stem: From the calibration run, what is the heat capacity of the calorimeter assembly?
questions.explanation: The standard released 26.4 kJ and the bath rose 2.64 °C, so C = q / ΔT = 26.4 / 2.64 = 10.0 kJ per °C. Dividing the heat by the temperature rise is the order that leaves the right units, kJ per degree.

wrong.A: 0.010 kJ/°C follows from reading the standard's heat as 26.4 J/g rather than kJ/g, a thousandfold slip in the unit.
wrong.B: 0.10 kJ/°C is the division taken the wrong way round, 2.64 divided by 26.4; that quantity has units of degrees per kilojoule.
wrong.C: 2.64 kJ/°C quotes the temperature rise itself as though it were the heat capacity, leaving the 26.4 kJ of heat unused.

questions.stem: How much energy does palmitic acid release per gram in this instrument?
questions.explanation: Palmitic acid raised the bath 3.90 °C, and each degree corresponds to 10.0 kJ, so the sample released 39.0 kJ. Because exactly 1.00 g was burned, that is also the energy per gram, 39.0 kJ/g.

wrong.A: 3.90 kJ/g is the temperature rise with a unit of energy attached; it still has to be multiplied by the calorimeter constant.
wrong.B: 15.6 kJ/g is the figure for glucose, whose rise was 1.56 °C, not for palmitic acid.
wrong.C: 29.7 kJ/g belongs to the ethanol row of Table 1, which produced a 2.97 °C rise.

questions.stem: Taking the molar mass of glucose as 180 g/mol, what is its molar heat of combustion?
questions.explanation: Glucose released 1.56 °C x 10.0 kJ/°C = 15.6 kJ per gram. One mole is 180 g, so a mole releases 15.6 × 180 = 2810 kJ, and the value is negative because combustion gives heat out: -2810 kJ/mol.

wrong.A: -15.6 kJ/mol is the energy per gram, not per mole; it has yet to be multiplied by the 180 g in a mole.
wrong.B: -281 kJ/mol multiplies the temperature rise by the molar mass without ever applying the 10.0 kJ/°C calorimeter constant.
wrong.D: -4000 kJ/mol uses 256 g/mol, the molar mass of palmitic acid, in place of the molar mass of glucose.

questions.stem: Why is the instrument calibrated by burning benzoic acid rather than by adding up the heat capacities of its parts?

choices.A: Benzoic acid burns cooler than the samples, which protects the steel vessel from damage.
choices.B: Burning the standard consumes the oxygen that would otherwise oxidise the walls of the vessel.
choices.C: The quantity needed is the heat capacity of vessel, stirrer and water acting together, which one combustion measures directly.
choices.D: Benzoic acid releases the same heat per gram as the samples, so the comparison cancels any error.

questions.explanation: The calorimeter constant is a property of the whole assembly: steel vessel, stirrer, thermometer and the water around them all absorb part of the heat. Burning a standard of known energy content and reading the rise measures that lumped quantity in one step, which is both easier and more accurate than estimating each part and summing them.

wrong.A: The combustion temperature of the standard is irrelevant to the measurement, and benzoic acid is chosen for the accuracy of its tabulated heat, not for burning gently.
wrong.B: The bomb is deliberately charged with oxygen in excess, so oxygen is never the limiting reagent and nothing is consumed on the walls.
wrong.D: Benzoic acid releases 26.4 kJ/g while the samples range from 15.6 to 39.0 kJ/g, so no cancellation of that kind takes place.

questions.stem: Which statement best explains why palmitic acid releases more energy per gram than glucose?

choices.A: Palmitic acid has the greater molar mass, so a gram of it holds more chemical bonds.
choices.B: Palmitic acid melts at the bath temperature, and the heat of fusion adds to the measured heat.
choices.C: Glucose dissolves in the water of the bath, so some of its energy is never released as heat.
choices.D: Almost all the carbon in palmitic acid is bonded only to hydrogen and carbon, so more of it remains to be oxidised.

questions.explanation: Combustion releases energy by converting C-H and C-C bonds into C=O and O-H bonds. Glucose already carries an oxygen on nearly every carbon, so much of that conversion has already happened; the hydrocarbon chain of a fatty acid has not been oxidised at all, which is why it yields 39.0 kJ/g against 15.6 kJ/g.

wrong.A: Energy per gram is independent of molar mass: dividing by mass removes the size of the molecule from the comparison.
wrong.B: Palmitic acid melts near 63 °C, well above the bath, and in any case a heat of fusion is far too small to explain a difference of this size.
wrong.C: The sample is burned inside a sealed vessel and never contacts the bath water, so it cannot dissolve in it.

questions.stem: What is the partial pressure of oxygen in humidified inspired gas at sea level?
questions.explanation: Removing the 47 mmHg of water vapour from 760 mmHg leaves 713 mmHg of dry gas, of which 21% is oxygen: 0.21 × 713 = 150 mmHg. Nothing in this step involves carbon dioxide, which only dilutes the oxygen later, inside the alveolus.

wrong.A: 100 mmHg is the alveolar value, after carbon dioxide has diluted the inspired gas; the question asks for the inspired partial pressure.
wrong.C: 160 mmHg takes 21% of the full 760 mmHg and so counts the 47 mmHg of water vapour as though it were air.
wrong.D: 713 mmHg is the pressure of the humidified gas as a whole and has not yet been multiplied by the oxygen fraction.

questions.stem: Using Table 1, what is the alveolar PO₂ of the volunteers resident at the clinic?
questions.explanation: Humidified inspired oxygen at the clinic is 0.21 × (460 mmHg less 47 mmHg) = 87 mmHg. The residents' PaCO₂ is 30 mmHg, so the dilution term is 30 / 0.8 = 37.5 mmHg, leaving an alveolar PO₂ of about 49 mmHg - roughly half the sea-level figure, which is why arterial saturation falls at altitude.

wrong.A: 12 mmHg subtracts the carbon dioxide correction twice over; the equation applies it once.
wrong.B: 37 mmHg uses the sea-level PaCO₂ of 40 mmHg. The residents have hyperventilated their PaCO₂ down to 30 mmHg, which is the value in their own row of the table.
wrong.D: 57 mmHg subtracts PaCO₂ itself rather than PaCO₂ divided by the exchange ratio of 0.8, and so understates the dilution.

questions.stem: What volume will the 20 mL pleural gas pocket occupy once the patient reaches the clinic?
questions.explanation: At constant temperature and fixed quantity of gas, PV is constant, so V2 = V1 × P₁/P₂ = 20 mL x 760/460 = 33 mL. Pressure has fallen, so the volume must rise, and the pocket grows by about two thirds.

wrong.A: 12 mL inverts the pressure ratio, multiplying by 460/760 instead of 760/460, and so predicts that the pocket shrinks as pressure falls.
wrong.B: 20 mL would require the gas to be unaffected by the fall in surrounding pressure, which Boyle's law rules out for a compliant pocket.
wrong.D: 55 mL applies the pressure ratio twice, as though volume varied with the square of the pressure.

questions.stem: Which change would have the LEAST effect on the alveolar PO₂ of a resident at the clinic?

choices.A: A rise in the saturated water vapour pressure from 47 to 50 mmHg with a fever.
choices.B: A fall in arterial PCO₂ from 30 to 20 mmHg on further hyperventilation.
choices.C: A fall in the respiratory exchange ratio from 0.8 to 0.6 on a fat-rich diet.
choices.D: A storm that lowers the barometric pressure at the clinic from 460 to 440 mmHg.

questions.explanation: Water vapour enters the calculation only through the subtraction from barometric pressure, and it is then multiplied by the oxygen fraction: three more mmHg of vapour costs 0.21 × 3, about 0.6 mmHg of alveolar oxygen. Every other change here moves the result by several mmHg at least, so the fever matters least.

wrong.B: Dropping PaCO₂ from 30 to 20 mmHg cuts the dilution term from 37.5 to 25 mmHg and so raises alveolar PO₂ by about 12 mmHg - the largest effect listed.
wrong.C: A ratio of 0.6 raises the dilution term from 37.5 to 50 mmHg, lowering alveolar PO₂ by about 12 mmHg.
wrong.D: Losing 20 mmHg of barometric pressure costs 0.21 × 20, about 4 mmHg of alveolar oxygen, several times the effect of the fever.

questions.stem: What is the pH of the solution after 12.5 mL of titrant has been added?
questions.explanation: The first equivalence point is at 25.0 mL, so 12.5 mL is the midpoint of the first rise: the alpha-carboxyl group is half deprotonated and the two forms are present in equal amounts. The log term is then zero and the pH equals that group's pKa, 1.8.

wrong.A: 0.9 halves the pKa itself. Half-equivalence means equal amounts of the two forms, which sets pH equal to the pKa rather than to half of it.
wrong.C: 6.0 is the pKa of the imidazole side chain, reached at 37.5 mL, the midpoint of the second rise.
wrong.D: 9.2 is the pKa of the alpha-amino group, reached at 62.5 mL, the midpoint of the third rise.

questions.stem: What is the pH of the solution after 62.5 mL of titrant has been added?
questions.explanation: The second equivalence point is at 50.0 mL and the third at 75.0 mL, so 62.5 mL is the midpoint between them. There the alpha-amino group is half deprotonated, the log term vanishes, and the pH equals its pKa of 9.2.

wrong.B: 7.6 is the isoelectric point of histidine. It is a property of the molecule, not a point reached at any particular titrant volume.
wrong.C: 6.0 is the pKa of the imidazole group, whose midpoint is at 37.5 mL, a full equivalence earlier.
wrong.D: 1.8 is the pKa of the alpha-carboxyl group, half titrated at 12.5 mL and completely titrated long before 62.5 mL.

questions.stem: What is the isoelectric point of histidine?
questions.explanation: The neutral species appears once the carboxyl group has lost its proton and before the amino group loses its own, so it is bracketed by the imidazole pKa of 6.0 and the amino pKa of 9.2. Averaging the two bracketing values gives (6.0 + 9.2)/2 = 7.6.

wrong.A: 3.9 averages the first two pKa values, 1.8 and 6.0. Those bracket the singly positive species, not the neutral one, because the side chain of histidine is basic.
wrong.B: 5.7 is the mean of all three pKa values, which has no physical meaning here; only the pair that brackets the neutral form counts.
wrong.C: 6.0 is a single pKa value. The isoelectric point of a molecule with three ionisable groups is never one of the pKa values itself.

questions.stem: After 37.5 mL of titrant has been added, which of the following are true? I. The imidazole side chain is half protonated. II. The alpha-carboxyl group is essentially fully deprotonated. III. The alpha-amino group has begun to lose its proton.
questions.explanation: At 37.5 mL the titration is halfway between the first and second equivalence points, so the group being titrated, the imidazole ring, is half protonated and statement I holds. The carboxyl group was fully titrated by 25.0 mL, so statement II holds as well. The pH there is 6.0, more than three units below the amino pKa of 9.2, so that group is still essentially completely protonated and statement III fails.

wrong.A: This omits statement II. The carboxyl group took the first equivalent of base, so by 25.0 mL it has already been deprotonated.
wrong.C: Statement III fails: at pH 6.0 the ratio of deprotonated to protonated amino groups is about 1 in 1600, so no measurable fraction has lost its proton.
wrong.D: Statements I and II both hold, but the alpha-amino group is not titrated until after the second equivalence point, so III cannot be included.

questions.stem: If the second rise in the curve does belong to the imidazole ring, what should the student's titration of the methyl analogue show?

choices.A: All three rises shifted to higher pH, with the spacing between them preserved.
choices.B: Four equivalence points rather than three, the extra one from the methyl group.
choices.C: The first equivalence point moved from 25.0 mL to 50.0 mL.
choices.D: Two equivalence points, with no buffering region near pH 6.

questions.explanation: Replacing the imidazole ring with an unreactive methyl group removes one ionisable group. The analogue then takes two equivalents of base instead of three, so its curve shows two equivalence points, and the plateau whose midpoint sat at pH 6.0 disappears. That is exactly the result that would assign the second rise to the side chain.

wrong.A: Removing a group does not shift the pKa values of the two that remain, and a shift of all three would leave the number of rises unchanged.
wrong.B: A methyl group has no acidic proton, so it cannot consume titrant or add an equivalence point.
wrong.C: The first equivalence point is set by the amount of analyte and the titrant concentration, both unchanged, so it stays at 25.0 mL.

questions.stem: Which statement describes the electron transfer in this titration correctly?

choices.A: Ascorbic acid is reduced, gaining two electrons from each iodine molecule.
choices.B: Iodine is oxidised to iodide, releasing two electrons to the ascorbic acid.
choices.C: Ascorbic acid is oxidised, and each iodine molecule gains the two electrons released.
choices.D: Starch is oxidised at the endpoint, and that reaction is what produces the blue colour.

questions.explanation: Ascorbic acid is the reducing agent: it gives up two electrons and becomes dehydroascorbic acid. Those electrons go to iodine, which is reduced to two iodide ions. The titrant is therefore the oxidising agent, and one mole of it matches one mole of ascorbic acid.

wrong.A: This reverses the roles. A reducing agent loses electrons; ascorbic acid is the reductant here, so it cannot be the species gaining them.
wrong.B: Iodine gains electrons on the way to iodide, which is reduction. Oxidation would mean a rise in oxidation state, not the fall from 0 to -1 that occurs.
wrong.D: The blue colour is a physical complex of iodine with the starch helix, not a redox reaction; starch is added as an indicator, not as a reactant.

questions.stem: Using the mean titre, how many moles of ascorbic acid were present in the 25.00 mL aliquot?
questions.explanation: The three titres average to 14.20 mL. Moles of iodine delivered are 0.0100 mol/L x 0.01420 L = 1.42 × 10⁻⁴ mol, and because ascorbic acid and iodine react in a one-to-one ratio the aliquot held 1.42 × 10⁻⁴ mol of ascorbic acid.

wrong.A: 7.10 × 10⁻⁵ mol halves the iodine figure, as though two moles of iodine were needed per mole of ascorbic acid. Two electrons are transferred, but one iodine molecule accepts both.
wrong.C: 2.84 × 10⁻⁴ mol doubles the iodine figure instead, which would require each iodine molecule to oxidise two ascorbic acid molecules.
wrong.D: 1.42 × 10⁻³ mol is a decade too large: the burette reading is 14.20 mL, which is 0.01420 L, not 0.1420 L.

questions.stem: What mass of ascorbic acid did the whole tablet contain?
questions.explanation: The aliquot was one quarter of the 100.0 mL solution, so the tablet held 4 × 1.42 × 10⁻⁴ = 5.68 × 10⁻⁴ mol. Multiplying by 176.1 g/mol gives 0.1000 g, that is 100.0 mg of ascorbic acid.

wrong.A: 25.0 mg is the mass in the aliquot alone and ignores that only a quarter of the tablet's solution was titrated.
wrong.B: 50.0 mg follows from assuming two moles of iodine per mole of ascorbic acid, which halves the moles found before the dilution factor is applied.
wrong.D: 400.0 mg applies the factor of four twice, once to the moles and again to the mass.

questions.stem: A technician instead uses an iodine solution standardised a month earlier and still labelled 0.0100 M. How would the reported content of the tablet be affected?

choices.A: Overstated, because the weaker solution needs a larger volume that is costed at the label concentration.
choices.B: Understated, because the endpoint arrives before all the ascorbic acid has reacted.
choices.C: Unchanged, because the same bottle was used for all three trials of the titration.
choices.D: Impossible to judge, because starch does not form its complex with an aged iodine solution.

questions.explanation: An iodine solution loses strength on standing, so its true concentration is below the 0.0100 M on the label. A weaker titrant takes a larger volume to reach the endpoint, and multiplying that larger volume by the label concentration credits the tablet with more ascorbic acid than it holds. The direction of the error is the point: standardising on the day of use removes it.

wrong.B: A weaker titrant delays the endpoint rather than bringing it forward, so if anything the volume is too large, which cannot understate the result.
wrong.C: Using one bottle throughout makes the three trials agree with each other, but a systematic error in its concentration shifts all three together and precision is not accuracy.
wrong.D: Starch forms its blue complex with whatever iodine is present, so the indicator still works; only the assumed concentration is wrong.

questions.stem: Which protocol subjects the sample to the greatest relative centrifugal force?
questions.explanation: The field goes as ω² r, so speed counts twice and radius once. Protocol 4 pairs the highest speed in the table with the larger of the two radii used at that speed, and no other row combines both: it reaches about 1.5 × 10³ times g, while protocols 2 and 3 reach about 755 times g and protocol 1 about 168 times g.

wrong.A: Protocol 1 has the lowest speed of the four, and speed is the term that is squared, so it gives the weakest field of all.
wrong.B: Protocol 2 shares the highest speed but at half the radius of protocol 4, which halves the field.
wrong.C: Protocol 3 has the largest radius, but its speed is half that of protocol 4, and halving the speed cuts the field fourfold.

questions.stem: What relative centrifugal force, as a multiple of g, does Protocol 4 apply?
questions.explanation: 3000 rpm is 50 revolutions per second, so ω = 2 π x 50 = 314 rad/s. Then ω² r = 314² x 0.15 = 1.48 × 10⁴ m/s², and dividing by g = 9.8 m/s² gives about 1.5 × 10³ times g, a figure typical of a clinical bench spin.

wrong.B: 1.5 × 10⁴ is the acceleration in m/s². A relative centrifugal force is that acceleration divided by g, which this choice omits.
wrong.C: 1.5 × 10⁵ leaves the radius in centimetres. The formula needs SI units, so 15 cm has to be entered as 0.15 m.
wrong.D: 5.4 × 10⁶ uses 3000 directly as revolutions per second. A speed in revolutions per minute must be divided by 60 first.

questions.stem: Which two protocols apply the same relative centrifugal force as each other?
questions.explanation: Protocol 3 runs at half the speed of protocol 2, which cuts ω² to a quarter, but at four times the radius, which restores the product. Both come to about 755 times g, and the pair illustrates that a slow wide rotor and a fast narrow one can be interchangeable.

wrong.A: Protocol 1 reaches about 168 times g and protocol 2 about 755 times g, a factor of four or so apart.
wrong.B: Protocols 1 and 4 share a radius but differ threefold in speed, so their fields differ about ninefold.
wrong.C: Protocols 2 and 4 share a speed but differ twofold in radius, so protocol 4 applies about twice the field.

questions.stem: Two organelle populations differ in density by only about 2%. Which change to a protocol would best separate them?

choices.A: Raise the speed to the highest the rotor will take, so the denser population reaches the bottom first.
choices.B: Spin longer at a moderate speed with the sample layered over a density gradient.
choices.C: Halve the rotor radius while keeping the speed unchanged, which sharpens the boundary.
choices.D: Warm the medium to lower its viscosity, so both populations sediment more freely.

questions.explanation: Raising the field speeds both populations, and with densities 2% apart both end up pelleted together. What distinguishes them is where each stops being denser than its surroundings, so a gradient that spans the two densities halts each at its own level, and a long moderate spin gives them time to reach it. The experiment is designed around the difference between the populations rather than around the size of the field.

wrong.A: A stronger field drives both populations to the bottom of the tube, which is the outcome being avoided; with a 2% difference the denser one arrives only marginally sooner.
wrong.C: Halving the radius merely halves the field and does nothing to the relative behaviour of the two populations.
wrong.D: Lowering the viscosity speeds both populations in nearly equal proportion, so their separation is no better and may be worse.

questions.stem: What is the peak blood velocity in Vessel C?
questions.explanation: Rearranging gives v = Δf c / (2 f₀ cosθ). With Δf = 3250 Hz, c = 1540 m/s, f₀ = 5.0 MHz and cosθ = 0.50, the denominator is 2 × 5.0 × 10⁶ x 0.50 = 5.0 × 10⁶, and 3250 × 1540 / (5.0 × 10⁶ = 1.00 m/s - a normal peak for a large artery.

wrong.B: 0.58 m/s uses sin 60°, 0.866, in place of cos 60°. The formula carries the cosine of the angle between the beam and the flow.
wrong.C: 0.50 m/s drops the cosine altogether, which is the velocity that would be reported if the beam lay along the vessel.
wrong.D: 0.40 m/s is the velocity in Vessel B, whose shift of 1300 Hz is a fifth of the value asked about.

questions.stem: What is the wavelength of the 5.0 MHz beam in soft tissue?
questions.explanation: Wavelength is speed divided by frequency: 1540 m/s divided by 5.0 × 10⁶ Hz is 3.1 × 10⁻⁴ m, which is 0.31 mm. That figure is also the scale of the finest detail the beam can resolve along its own axis.

wrong.A: 0.031 mm is a decade too small; 1540 divided by 5.0 × 10⁶ is 3.1 × 10⁻⁴ m, not 3.1 × 10⁻⁵ m.
wrong.B: 0.15 mm halves the wavelength, borrowing the factor of two that belongs to the round trip of the Doppler shift rather than to the wavelength.
wrong.D: 3.1 mm is a decade too large and would make the beam unable to resolve any vessel wall.

questions.stem: Which change would NOT increase the frequency shift recorded from a given vessel?

choices.A: Fitting a 7.5 MHz probe in place of the 5.0 MHz probe.
choices.B: Tilting the probe so the beam meets the flow at 75° rather than 60°.
choices.C: Recording at peak systole rather than at end-diastole.
choices.D: Sampling within a stenosis, where the same flow passes through a narrower lumen.

questions.explanation: The shift is proportional to the cosine of the angle, and the cosine falls as the angle grows toward 90°: from 0.50 at 60° to 0.26 at 75°. Tilting the beam further off the line of flow therefore cuts the shift roughly in half. Every other change listed raises either the probe frequency or the blood velocity, both of which raise the shift.

wrong.A: The shift is directly proportional to f₀, so a 7.5 MHz probe returns half again as much shift from the same velocity.
wrong.C: Blood moves fastest at peak systole, and the shift is proportional to velocity, so the recorded shift rises.
wrong.D: Continuity requires the velocity to rise where the lumen narrows, so the same flow gives a larger shift inside a stenosis.

questions.stem: The technician's goniometer reads 60°, but the beam in fact meets the flow at 70°. What is the consequence for the reported velocity?

choices.A: It is about a third too low, because the true cosine is smaller than the one assumed.
choices.B: It is about a third too high, because a larger angle returns a larger frequency shift.
choices.C: It is unaffected, because the angle error cancels between the outgoing pulse and the echo.
choices.D: It is too low by the ratio 60/70, since the error is proportional to the angle itself.

questions.explanation: The instrument divides the measured shift by the cosine it has been told to assume. The true cosine at 70° is 0.342 against the assumed 0.500, so the true velocity is larger than the reported one by 0.500/0.342, and the report falls short by about 32%. This is why the angle is recorded with the measurement and why practice keeps it well below 90°, where the error grows without limit.

wrong.B: A larger angle returns a smaller shift, not a larger one, because the cosine falls; the reported velocity is therefore too low rather than too high.
wrong.C: The factor of two accounts for the double shift, but the angle enters both legs the same way, so nothing about it cancels.
wrong.D: The error depends on the ratio of the cosines, not on the ratio of the angles; 60/70 would predict a 14% shortfall rather than 32%.

questions.stem: What fraction of an administered technetium-99m dose is still active 18 hours later?
questions.explanation: The half-life is 6.0 h, so 18 hours is three half-lives. Each one halves the activity, and halving three times leaves 1/8 of the dose. The arithmetic needs no exponentials once the elapsed time is counted in half-lives.

wrong.A: 1/16 counts four half-lives, which would take 24 hours rather than 18.
wrong.C: 1/4 counts two half-lives, which is only 12 hours of decay.
wrong.D: 1/2 counts a single half-life and so credits the nuclide with 6 hours of decay instead of 18.

questions.stem: What activity remains in the fluorine-18 vial when the patient is finally injected?
questions.explanation: The half-life is 110 min, so 220 minutes is exactly two half-lives. The activity falls to 400 × (1/2)² = 100 MBq, a quarter of the assayed value, which is why a delayed scan may need a fresh vial.

wrong.A: 283 MBq is 400 divided by the square root of two, the activity after half of one half-life rather than after two.
wrong.B: 200 MBq counts one half-life only, as though 110 minutes had elapsed instead of 220.
wrong.C: 141 MBq corresponds to one and a half half-lives, that is 165 minutes, not 220.

questions.stem: What is the decay constant of gallium-68?
questions.explanation: For a first-order process k = ln 2 / T. With T = 68 min, k = 0.693 / 68 = 1.0 × 10⁻² per minute, so about 1% of the remaining nuclei decay each minute.

wrong.B: 1.5 × 10⁻² per minute is 1/68, which omits the factor of ln 2 that links a half-life to a rate constant.
wrong.C: 6.1 × 10⁻¹ is the value per hour, 0.693 × 60 / 68, carrying the wrong unit of time.
wrong.D: 4.7 × 10¹ multiplies ln 2 by the half-life instead of dividing by it, which inverts the units as well as the size.

questions.stem: Which of the following are disadvantages of iodine-131 for routine diagnostic imaging? I. Its half-life keeps the patient irradiated for weeks after the image has been taken. II. Its beta particles deposit energy in tissue without contributing to the image. III. Its photons are absorbed inside the body before they can reach a detector.
questions.explanation: A half-life of 8.0 days leaves about 30% of the activity still present a fortnight after the scan, so statement I holds. Table 1 gives beta particles among its emissions, and the passage notes that they are absorbed within millimetres of tissue, delivering dose but no signal, so statement II holds too. Statement III fails: iodine-131 also emits gamma photons, which do leave the body, and the nuclide is imaged routinely in therapy follow-up for exactly that reason.

wrong.A: This omits statement II, but the beta emissions listed in the table are the main reason iodine-131 is reserved for therapy rather than diagnosis.
wrong.C: Statement III is false: the gamma component escapes the body readily, which is what allows post-therapy scans at all.
wrong.D: Statements I and II hold, but including III would mean the nuclide could not be imaged, contradicting its established use.

questions.stem: What is the gauge pressure inside the saline-lined model alveolus?
questions.explanation: Laplace's law gives P = 2γ/r with γ = 50 mN/m = 0.050 N/m and r = 50 micrometres = 5.0 × 10⁻⁵ m. So P = 2 × 0.050 / (5.0 × 10⁻⁵ = 2000 Pa, around 15 mmHg, which is far more than the pressure a breath could overcome.

wrong.B: 1000 Pa omits the factor of two in Laplace's law, which comes from the two directions of curvature of a sphere.
wrong.C: 500 Pa belongs to the surfactant-lined alveolus at full inflation, with a tension of 25 mN/m and twice the radius.
wrong.D: 400 Pa is the surfactant-lined alveolus at end-expiration, whose tension is a fifth of the saline value.

questions.stem: Expressed in mmHg, what is the gauge pressure in the surfactant-lined alveolus at end-expiration? (1 mmHg = 133 Pa)
questions.explanation: With γ = 10 mN/m = 0.010 N/m and r = 5.0 × 10⁻⁵ m, Laplace's law gives 2 × 0.010 / (5.0 × 10⁻⁵ = 400 Pa. Dividing by 133 Pa per mmHg gives 3.0 mmHg, which is the order of pressure a quiet breath can supply.

wrong.A: 15.0 mmHg is the 2000 Pa of the saline-lined film and uses the tension of a surface with no surfactant on it.
wrong.B: 7.5 mmHg comes from pairing the full-inflation tension of 25 mN/m with the end-expiratory radius of 50 micrometres; the table pairs that tension with 100 micrometres.
wrong.C: 3.8 mmHg is the 500 Pa of the fully inflated alveolus, whose radius is twice the one asked about.

questions.stem: How does surfactant lower the surface tension of the alveolar lining?

choices.A: It thickens the lining fluid, and the greater viscosity resists the inward pull.
choices.B: It warms the film, which weakens hydrogen bonding throughout the bulk liquid.
choices.C: Its amphipathic molecules occupy the surface and interrupt hydrogen bonding between the water molecules there.
choices.D: It reacts with water at the surface, replacing hydrogen bonds with covalent bonds.

questions.explanation: Surface tension arises because water molecules at a surface are held by their neighbours below and to the side but not above. A surfactant molecule sits at that interface with its tails in the gas and its head group in the water, taking up surface area that water molecules would otherwise occupy and breaking up the hydrogen-bonded network there. Fewer water-water interactions at the surface means less tension.

wrong.A: Viscosity governs how fast a fluid flows, not how strongly its surface contracts; a thicker film has the same surface tension.
wrong.B: Surfactant does not change the temperature of the film, and the effect is a surface phenomenon rather than a change in the bulk liquid.
wrong.D: No covalent bonds form. The interaction is the ordinary physical association of an amphipathic molecule with an interface.

questions.stem: Two alveoli of unequal radius share a duct. Why does the smaller not simply empty into the larger?

choices.A: Compression of the surfactant film in the smaller alveolus lowers its tension, and so its pressure.
choices.B: The lining fluid is thicker in the smaller alveolus, and that resists flow out of it.
choices.C: Laplace's law does not hold for alveoli that are connected to each other.
choices.D: Once surfactant is present the internal pressure no longer depends on the radius at all.

questions.explanation: At a fixed surface tension the smaller sphere is at higher pressure and would indeed discharge into the larger. Surfactant breaks that logic: the smaller alveolus has the more compressed film, its tension is lower, and the fall in tension offsets the fall in radius in P = 2γ/r, so the two pressures stay close and both stay open.

wrong.B: Film thickness is not what Laplace's law depends on; the pressure is set by tension and radius, and a thicker film would not stop a pressure difference from driving flow.
wrong.C: Laplace's law applies to each alveolus whatever it is connected to; the connection is what makes the pressure difference matter.
wrong.D: The radius still enters the relation with surfactant present. What changes is that the tension varies with radius as well, which weakens the dependence rather than abolishing it.

questions.stem: How much energy does the adult module store at its standard setting?
questions.explanation: U = (1/2) C V² with C = 100 microfarads = 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ F and V = 2000 V. Then U = 0.5 × 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ x (2000)² = 200 J, which is the standard adult dose quoted in practice.

wrong.A: 0.10 J leaves the voltage unsquared, computing (1/2) C V instead of (1/2) C V².
wrong.B: 0.20 J is the charge on the capacitor in coulombs, CV, reported as though it were an energy.
wrong.C: 100 J is the energy of the lower setting, which this machine reaches by charging to 1.4 kV rather than 2.0 kV.

questions.stem: What charge sits on the adult capacitor at its standard setting?
questions.explanation: Q = CV = 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ F x 2000 V = 2.0 × 10⁻¹ C. Two tenths of a coulomb delivered in a few milliseconds is a current of tens of amperes, which is what the myocardium actually responds to.

wrong.A: 1.0 × 10⁻¹ C carries the factor of one half across from the energy formula; the charge is CV with no such factor.
wrong.C: 2.7 × 10⁻¹ C uses 2.7 kV, the voltage of the 360 J setting, rather than the standard 2.0 kV.
wrong.D: 2.0 × 10⁵ C treats the capacitance as 100 F. The module is 100 microfarads, which is 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ F.

questions.stem: What is the time constant of the adult module discharging through the chest?
questions.explanation: The time constant of a resistor and capacitor in series is their product: 50 ohm x 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ F = 5.0 × 10⁻³ s, that is 5 ms. The discharge is therefore over in roughly 20 ms, which matches the few-millisecond pulse the passage describes.

wrong.A: 2.5 × 10⁻³ s uses the paediatric module's 50 microfarads rather than the adult module's 100 microfarads.
wrong.C: 1.0 × 10⁻² s uses the 200 microfarads of the parallel pair, not the single adult capacitor.
wrong.D: 5.0 × 10³ s treats the capacitance as 100 F; forgetting the μ prefix stretches a 5 ms pulse into well over an hour.

questions.stem: The engineer wires the two adult capacitors in parallel and charges them to 2.0 kV. What energy is stored?
questions.explanation: Capacitances in parallel add, so the pair is 200 microfarads = 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ F at the same 2.0 kV. Then U = 0.5 × 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ x (2000)² = 400 J: doubling the capacitance at a fixed voltage doubles the stored energy.

wrong.A: 100 J is the result for the two capacitors in series, where the reciprocals add and the pair behaves as 50 microfarads.
wrong.B: 200 J is the energy of a single adult capacitor and ignores the second one entirely.
wrong.D: 800 J doubles the energy a second time, as though the voltage had been doubled as well as the capacitance.

questions.stem: Which of the following changes would increase the energy a module stores? I. Doubling its capacitance at the same charging voltage. II. Doubling the charging voltage at the same capacitance. III. Connecting a second identical capacitor in parallel with it at the same charging voltage.
questions.explanation: Energy is (1/2) C V², so it rises with either factor. Doubling the capacitance doubles it, and statement I holds. Doubling the voltage quadruples it, so statement II holds. Adding an identical capacitor in parallel doubles the capacitance, which is statement I by another route, so statement III holds as well.

wrong.A: This omits statement II, but the energy depends on the square of the voltage, so doubling the voltage raises the stored energy most of all.
wrong.B: Statement III also holds: parallel capacitances add, so the pair stores twice the energy of one at the same voltage.
wrong.C: Statement II holds and cannot be left out; raising the charging voltage is how the machine changes its dose.

questions.stem: What rate law do the data in Table 1 support?

choices.A: First order in the bromide and first order in the thiol
choices.B: First order in the bromide and zero order in the thiol
choices.C: Second order in the bromide and zero order in the thiol
choices.D: First order in the bromide and second order in the thiol

questions.explanation: Comparing trials 1 and 2, doubling the bromide at fixed thiol doubles the rate, so the order in the bromide is one. Comparing trials 1 and 3, doubling the thiol at fixed bromide also doubles the rate, so the order in the thiol is one as well. Trial 4, with both doubled and the rate four times trial 1, confirms the pair.

wrong.B: Zero order in the thiol would mean the rate was unchanged between trials 1 and 3, but it doubles.
wrong.C: Second order in the bromide would mean a fourfold rise between trials 1 and 2, where the rate only doubles.
wrong.D: Second order in the thiol would require a fourfold rise between trials 1 and 3, and would make trial 4 eight times trial 1 rather than four times.

questions.stem: What is the rate constant for the primary drug?
questions.explanation: With the rate law first order in each reactant, k = rate / ([RBr][RSH]). Using trial 1, k = 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ / (0.10 × 0.10) = 2.0 × 10⁻² per molar per second. Any of the four trials gives the same value, which is itself a check on the rate law.

wrong.B: 5.0 × 10⁻³ pairs the rate of trial 1 with the concentrations of trial 4, mixing rows of the table.
wrong.C: 2.0 × 10⁻³ divides by one concentration only, which would be the rate constant for a reaction first order overall.
wrong.D: 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ is the measured rate of trial 1 reported as a rate constant; it has not been divided by any concentration.

questions.stem: What does the rate law imply about the mechanism for the primary drug?

choices.A: A unimolecular ionisation, with the thiol capturing the carbocation afterwards
choices.B: A radical chain, initiated by loss of a hydrogen atom from the thiol
choices.C: An elimination to an alkene, to which the thiol then adds
choices.D: A bimolecular displacement, the thiol attacking carbon as bromide leaves

questions.explanation: Both species appear in the rate law to the first power, so both are present in the transition state of the rate-determining step. That is the bimolecular displacement: the thiol attacks the carbon from the side opposite the bromide, and the bond to sulfur forms as the bond to bromine breaks. A primary alkyl bromide is the substrate this route handles best, because the carbon is least hindered.

wrong.A: A unimolecular ionisation would make the rate independent of the thiol, yet doubling the thiol doubles the rate.
wrong.B: A radical chain would not give clean first-order dependence on each reactant, and nothing here initiates radicals.
wrong.C: An elimination would have to compete with substitution and would show base dependence of a different kind; it also cannot explain the thiol appearing to the first power in a single step.

questions.stem: The tertiary analogue's rate does not change when the thiol concentration is doubled. Which conclusion does that best support?

choices.A: Its rate-determining step involves the substrate alone.
choices.B: It does not react with the thiol at all under these conditions.
choices.C: The thiol is a stronger nucleophile toward tertiary carbon than toward primary carbon.
choices.D: It reacts by the same bimolecular route as the primary drug, only faster.

questions.explanation: A reagent that does not appear in the rate law is not present in the rate-determining step. Since doubling the thiol leaves the rate alone, the slow step must involve the tertiary substrate by itself, which is the ionisation to a carbocation; the thiol is consumed in a fast step afterwards. The thirty-fold rate rise fits the same picture, since a tertiary carbocation is the more stable.

wrong.B: It plainly does react, and faster than the primary compound; what the data show is that the thiol is absent from the slow step, not from the reaction.
wrong.C: Nucleophile strength is a property of the thiol and would show up as a dependence on its concentration, which is exactly what is missing.
wrong.D: A bimolecular route would make the rate proportional to the thiol concentration, so the rate would have doubled.

questions.stem: The primary drug is run again at 0.40 M in the bromide and 0.050 M in the thiol. What initial rate should be expected?
questions.explanation: With the rate law first order in each reactant, rate = k[RBr][RSH]. Using the constant from the table, 2.0 × 10⁻² x 0.40 × 0.050 = 4.0 × 10⁻⁴ M/s. Raising the bromide fourfold and lowering the thiol by half changes the product of the concentrations by a factor of two, so the rate is twice that of trial 1.

wrong.A: 1.6 × 10⁻⁴ M/s makes the reaction second order in the bromide, computing k[RBr]²[RSH]; the data show the order in the bromide is one.
wrong.B: 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ M/s is the rate of trial 1 and assumes the two changes cancel, but quadrupling one concentration while halving the other doubles their product.
wrong.D: 1.0 × 10⁻³ M/s drops the bromide term and computes k[RSH] alone, which would be the rate law only if the bromide were zero order.

questions.stem: Normal saline is 0.154 M NaCl. What osmotic pressure does it exert at 37 °C across a membrane permeable to water alone? (R = 0.0821 L atm mol⁻¹ K⁻¹
questions.explanation: Osmotic pressure is i M R T, and sodium chloride dissociates into two particles, so i = 2. Then 2 × 0.154 × 0.0821 × 310 = 7.8 atm. The figure is large because osmotic pressure counts particles, not mass, and it is the reason an isotonic fluid is prescribed by concentration rather than by volume.

wrong.A: 794 is the answer in kilopascals, obtained with R = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹, mislabelled as atmospheres.
wrong.C: 3.9 atm takes i = 1, treating dissolved sodium chloride as though it stayed as intact units rather than separating into two ions.
wrong.D: 0.94 atm uses 37 for the temperature. The gas constant requires kelvin, so 37 °C must be entered as 310 K.

questions.stem: Which aqueous solution has the LOWEST freezing point?
questions.explanation: Freezing point depression depends on the total concentration of dissolved particles. Calcium chloride releases three ions per formula unit, so 0.10 M CaCl₂ is about 0.30 M in particles, a higher particle concentration than any other solution listed, and it therefore depresses the freezing point the most.

wrong.A: Glucose does not ionise, so 0.10 M glucose is 0.10 M in particles, the lowest of the four.
wrong.B: Acetic acid is a weak acid and only a few percent ionises, so its particle concentration is barely above 0.10 M.
wrong.D: Sodium chloride gives two ions per formula unit, about 0.20 M in particles, which is less than calcium chloride provides.

questions.stem: A mixture is separated by reverse-phase chromatography on a nonpolar C18 stationary phase eluted with a polar water and methanol mixture. Which component is retained longest?

choices.A: The component with the most hydroxyl groups
choices.B: The component with the longest unbranched alkyl chain
choices.C: The component with the lowest molar mass
choices.D: The component carrying a permanent negative charge

questions.explanation: In reverse phase the stationary phase is the nonpolar one, so retention tracks affinity for a nonpolar environment. A long alkyl chain interacts with the C18 surface through dispersion forces along its whole length, so that component spends the most time on the column and elutes last.

wrong.A: Hydroxyl groups hydrogen bond with the aqueous eluent, which keeps the component in the mobile phase and brings it off early.
wrong.C: Molar mass by itself does not set retention in reverse phase; a small nonpolar molecule can be held longer than a large polar one.
wrong.D: A charged species is strongly solvated by the polar eluent and is among the first to leave the column.

questions.stem: Two proteins of similar mass have isoelectric points two pH units apart. Which technique separates them most directly?

choices.A: Size-exclusion chromatography in a neutral buffer
choices.B: Dialysis against a large volume of buffer
choices.C: Ion-exchange chromatography at a pH between the two values

questions.explanation: At a pH between the two isoelectric points, the protein with the lower value is above its own and carries net negative charge, while the other is below its own and carries net positive charge. An ion-exchange column then binds one and lets the other pass, which turns a difference in isoelectric point directly into a separation.

wrong.A: Size exclusion sorts by hydrodynamic size, and the two proteins have similar mass, so they would elute together.
wrong.B: Dialysis separates small molecules from large ones across a membrane; both proteins are retained on the same side.
wrong.D: Acidified methanol would denature both proteins and sorts by surface hydrophobicity, which has no fixed relation to isoelectric point.

questions.stem: Protons resonate at 42.58 MHz per tesla. At what frequency must the radiofrequency coil of a 1.5 T scanner be driven?
questions.explanation: The resonance frequency is proportional to the field: 42.58 MHz/T x 1.5 T = 63.9 MHz. That is why a scanner's coils are tuned to the field it runs at, and why images from a 1.5 T and a 3 T machine are acquired at different frequencies.

wrong.A: 42.6 MHz quotes the constant itself and has not been multiplied by the field strength.
wrong.C: 85.2 MHz uses 2.0 T rather than the 1.5 T of this scanner.
wrong.D: 95.8 MHz multiplies by the field twice over; the relation is linear in the field, not quadratic.

questions.stem: An optical fibre has a core of refractive index 1.50 and cladding of index 1.45. Measured from the normal, what is the critical angle at the core-cladding boundary?
questions.explanation: Total internal reflection sets in when the refracted ray would graze the boundary, so sinθ = n₂/n₁ = 1.45/1.50 = 0.967, giving θ = 75.2°. The angle is large because the two indices are close, which is exactly what confines light that enters the fibre nearly along its axis.

wrong.A: 14.8° is the complement of the critical angle, the angle measured from the boundary rather than from the normal.
wrong.B: 41.8° is the critical angle for this core against air, using a ratio of 1/1.50, and ignores the cladding.
wrong.C: 69.1° squares the ratio of the indices before taking the inverse sine; the relation uses the ratio itself.

questions.stem: A 5.0 kg mass is held in the hand with the forearm horizontal, 30 cm from the elbow joint. The biceps inserts 4.0 cm from the joint. Ignoring the weight of the forearm, what force must the biceps exert?
questions.explanation: Taking torques about the elbow, F x 0.040 m = 5.0 kg x 9.8 m/s² x 0.30 m, so F = 49 × 0.30 / 0.040 = 368 N. The muscle is at a mechanical disadvantage of about seven to one, which is the price paid for a short insertion that lets the hand move quickly.

wrong.A: 6.5 N interchanges the two lever arms, dividing by 0.30 m and multiplying by 0.040 m, and would mean the muscle had the advantage.
wrong.B: 49 N is the weight of the load alone and ignores that the load and the muscle act at different distances from the joint.
wrong.D: 3675 N is a decade too large: the insertion is 4.0 cm, which is 0.040 m rather than 0.0040 m.

questions.stem: The intensity of a sound rises by a factor of 100. By how much does its intensity level rise?
questions.explanation: Intensity level is 10 log(I/I0) in decibels, and log 100 = 2, so the level rises by 10 × 2 = 20 dB. Each tenfold rise in intensity adds 10 dB, and two of them add 20.

wrong.A: 2 dB is the logarithm itself, which still has to be multiplied by 10 to reach decibels.
wrong.B: 10 dB corresponds to a tenfold rise in intensity, not a hundredfold one.
wrong.D: 40 dB uses the factor 20, which belongs to the version of the formula written in terms of pressure amplitude rather than intensity.

questions.stem: An exothermic gas-phase reaction sits at equilibrium in a sealed vessel. The temperature is then raised. What happens?

choices.A: The equilibrium shifts toward reactants and the equilibrium constant falls.
choices.B: The equilibrium shifts toward products and the equilibrium constant rises.
choices.C: The equilibrium shifts toward products while the equilibrium constant stays the same.
choices.D: Neither the position of equilibrium nor the constant changes, since no substance was added.

questions.explanation: Heat is a product of an exothermic reaction, so adding heat drives the system back toward reactants. Temperature is also the one variable that changes the equilibrium constant itself: for an exothermic reaction K falls as temperature rises, which is why the yield of such a reaction is improved by cooling.

wrong.B: Shifting toward products on heating is the behaviour of an endothermic reaction, which absorbs heat.
wrong.C: A change in temperature does change the constant; only a change in concentration or pressure shifts the position at a fixed constant.
wrong.D: Temperature alters the constant directly, so nothing needs to be added for the equilibrium to move.

questions.stem: A buffer contains 0.10 M acetic acid, whose pKa is 4.76, and 0.050 M sodium acetate. What is its pH?
questions.explanation: The Henderson-Hasselbalch relation gives pH = pKa + log([A-]/[HA]) = 4.76 + log(0.050/0.10). The ratio is 0.50 and log 0.50 is -0.30, so the pH is 4.46: slightly below the pKa, as it must be when the acid form is in excess.

wrong.A: 4.16 doubles the log term, as though the ratio were 0.25 rather than 0.50.
wrong.C: 4.76 is the pKa, which is the pH only when the two forms are present in equal amounts.
wrong.D: 5.06 inverts the ratio and puts the base over the acid, which would raise the pH above the pKa.

questions.stem: A drug molecule has three stereocentres and no internal plane of symmetry. How many stereoisomers are possible?
questions.explanation: Each stereocentre can take either of two configurations independently, so the count is 2³ = 8 stereoisomers, which make up four pairs of enantiomers. The absence of internal symmetry is what rules out meso forms that would reduce the count.

wrong.A: 3 counts the stereocentres rather than the arrangements they can take.
wrong.B: 6 multiplies the number of centres by two, which would be right only if the centres could not vary independently of one another.
wrong.D: 9 squares the number of centres. The base of the power is the two configurations available, and the exponent is the number of centres.

questions.stem: Each of the following changes would speed the hydroxide-catalysed hydrolysis of a methyl ester EXCEPT

choices.A: replacing the methyl group on the acyl carbon with a tert-butyl group.
choices.B: raising the hydroxide concentration at constant temperature.
choices.C: replacing a methyl substituent on the acyl group with a trifluoromethyl group.

questions.explanation: Base-catalysed ester hydrolysis begins with hydroxide adding to the carbonyl carbon, so anything that crowds that carbon slows the reaction. A tert-butyl group beside the carbonyl is the bulkiest substituent offered and shields the carbon from attack, which is why hindered esters hydrolyse sluggishly. The other three changes all speed the reaction.

wrong.B: Hydroxide appears in the rate law of this reaction, so a higher concentration of it gives a faster rate.
wrong.C: A trifluoromethyl group withdraws electron density inductively, making the carbonyl carbon more electrophilic and more readily attacked.
wrong.D: A rise of 20 °C typically multiplies a rate of this kind several times over, since the rate constant rises steeply with temperature.

questions.stem: A drug is eliminated by a first-order process with a rate constant of 0.050 s⁻¹. What fraction of a dose remains 60 s after it is given?
questions.explanation: For first-order loss the fraction remaining is e raised to the power −kt. With k = 0.050 s⁻¹ and t = 60 s that exponent is −3, and e⁻³ is about 0.05, or 5%. The same result follows from the half-life: ln 2 / 0.050 is about 14 s, and 60 s is more than four half-lives, which leaves a twentieth or so.

wrong.B: 25% is what two half-lives would leave, that is about 28 s of elimination rather than 60 s.
wrong.C: 50% is one half-life of about 14 s, and treats the 60 s as though it were that interval.
wrong.D: 95% is the fraction eliminated, not the fraction remaining; the two are complements.

questions.stem: Which amino acid side chain carries a positive charge at pH 7.4?
questions.explanation: The side chain amine of lysine has a pKa near 10.5, so at pH 7.4 it is some three units below its pKa and is almost entirely protonated, carrying a positive charge. That charge is what lets lysine residues bind the phosphate backbone of DNA.

wrong.A: The aspartate side chain is a carboxylic acid with a pKa near 3.9, so at pH 7.4 it is deprotonated and negatively charged.
wrong.C: Serine carries a neutral hydroxyl group, which does not ionise appreciably until the pH is far above 7.4.
wrong.D: The phenol of tyrosine has a pKa near 10, so it is still protonated at pH 7.4 and therefore neutral, not positive.

questions.stem: For which process is the entropy change of the system negative?

choices.A: Condensation of steam to liquid water at 100 °C
choices.B: Sublimation of solid carbon dioxide at room temperature
choices.C: Dissolution of solid sodium chloride in water
choices.D: Thermal denaturation of a folded globular protein

questions.explanation: Entropy falls when a system's molecules lose access to arrangements. Condensation takes molecules from a gas, where they are free to move independently, into a liquid, where they are held among neighbours; far fewer arrangements remain, so the entropy change of the system is negative.

wrong.B: Sublimation takes a solid straight to a gas, the largest rise in available arrangements of any change listed.
wrong.C: Dissolution breaks an ordered lattice and disperses ions through the solvent, which raises the entropy of the system.
wrong.D: An unfolded chain samples an enormous number of conformations compared with a single folded structure, so denaturation raises the entropy.
